newsitem.title: GREECE: Leftist guerrillas shoot dead Greek shipowner.
newsitem.headline: Leftist guerrillas shoot dead Greek shipowner.

text.p: Members of Greece's November 17 urban guerrilla group shot dead shipowner Constantine Peratikos on Wednesday as he left his office and they fled in a hijacked taxi, police said.
Peratikos, 42, was ambushed in Piraeus, Greece's main port near Athens, as he was heading for a garage to get his car at about 5 p.m. (1500 GMT).
"Ballistic tests showed the pistol is the same used by November 17 in 11 attacks," a senior police officer told Reuters.
November 17 leftist guerrillas have killed 21 Greeks and foreigners -- including a U.S. Central Intelligence Agency station chief and a U.S. military attache -- since bursting into existence in 1975.
But it had been dormant since a bungled rocket attack on the U.S. embassy in January 1996.

Police found .45 calibre shells at the site of Wednesday's shooting. November 17 uses a trademark .45 calibre pistol as a signature to many of its attacks and is also versed in remote controlled bombs and rockets.
"This was the first indication that this could be a terrorist attack," police chief Athanassios Vassilopoulos told reporters at the scene.
Hospital officials said Peratikos was shot seven times and died before reaching Piraeus' Tzanio hospital.
The three gunmen nearly botched their escape when the van they planned to use failed to start, police said. So they hijacked a taxi passing by and sped away.
"I saw two of them as they were leaving. They had big guns. They seemed cool, as if they were well-trained," a shopowner told Greek television.
November 17's last fatal attack was against Turkish embassy Counsellor Omer Haluk Sipahioglu, who was shot by a three-man hit squad outside his home in June 1994.
The group made its debut with the same .45 calibre semi-automatic pistol, killing CIA station chief Richard Welch in December 1975. None of its members has ever been arrested.
"It is an extremely sad event. I express my sorrow and am awaiting a detailed report from the Public Order ministry," said Prime Minister Costas Simitis, referring to the latest attack.
November 17 named itself after the day in 1973 when Greece's then-ruling military junta used tanks to put down a student uprising.
The Peratikos Group, owned by one of Greece's major shipping families, bought the troubled Elefsis Shipyards in the early 1990s. But the shipyards have since reverted to state hands.
The Peratikos family own the Piraeus-based Aran Shipping and Trading company and the London-based Pegasus Ocean Services.
